This article is for the QA or statistical-programming lead who has to decide
whether the package can be used in a regulated setting. It says how
rtfreporter's own quality is assured, which documents carry the evidence,
and what is left for your company to do. The steps for your side are in
[Validating rtfreporter in your environment](validation.html).

The rules are in one document, the **Quality Plan**
(`inst/validation/quality-plan.md`). This article explains it. If the two
differ, the Quality Plan is right.

## The approach

### Risk-based

Not every combination of every argument can be tested, and not every one
needs to be. The package states its requirements where a wrong result would
reach your report. It states them most deeply where a mistake is likeliest
or hardest to see.

### What is required

The requirements are written from what the package says about itself: its
exported functions, the help of each, and the checks in the code. They are
the **Functional Requirements (FR)**. Each function has FRs of five kinds.

| Kind | What it states |
|---|---|
| `behaviour` | What the function does. |
| `argument` | What each meaningful value of an argument does. |
| `data` | A shape of data the function handles: no rows, one row, `NA`, factor levels, one or many groups, long or non-ASCII text. |
| `guard` | A misuse the package stops, and the error or warning it gives. An unintended use must stop. It must not produce a wrong file. |
| `interaction` | A risky combination: a precedence or an override, an argument that changes the meaning of another, a combination that once had a bug. |

Only the risky combinations are required. Pairwise combinations of all
arguments are not.

Tests check that the list is complete. A test fails when an exported
function has an argument that no FR names. It fails when the package reads
an option that no FR names. It fails when an FR has neither a test nor a
deviation. These checks do not show that the help is complete. An FR is only
as good as the reading that wrote it.

### Why passing the tests shows the requirements are met

Each test is mapped to the FRs it checks. A test counts for an FR only when
it asserts what the FR states: the value returned, the RTF written, or the
error given. A test that only calls a function does not count.

The tests use these designs.

- **Equivalence classes and boundaries** for arguments and data. One FR
  stands for a class of values that the function treats alike. A value at the
  edge of a rule gets its own FR.
- **Regression cases** for misuse and for past bugs. A fixed bug gets an FR
  and a test that names the issue.
- **Interaction FRs** for the few combinations that are a risk.
- **End-to-end scenarios** that run a whole program, from data to an RTF
  file. The test compares the file line by line with a reference RTF. The
  programs use fictional data and nothing that varies between runs.

Each mapping is checked by a person when it is made. The person reads the FR
and the test, and records that the test asserts the FR. The record quotes
the expectation lines as evidence (`traceability_review.csv`). A test fails
when a mapping has no such record.

### The expected result

A test needs an expected result that does not come from the code under test.
The tests take it from these sources:

- a rule in the help, worked out in the test's header;
- a calculation by hand, such as the pages of ten rows, or a column's width
  from the glyph widths of the font;
- the same table made by a direct call, which a plan must match;
- input built by hand, so that the result is known by construction.

The reference RTF files are different. The package wrote them. They show
that the output has not changed. They do not show that it was right. So a
person reads each reference, control word by control word (page setup,
fonts, cell widths, borders, alignment, the text), and records the reading
(`reference_review.csv`). What only a person can judge, such as how Word lays
out the page, stays marked `pending-human` until someone has looked. The
references show stability. The other sources show correctness.

### Coverage is an aid

Line coverage shows which lines no test runs. It cannot show that a test
checks what a line does. It cannot see a requirement that has no code. So it
helps to find untested code, and it never counts for an FR. The Quality
Report states the figure of the release.

### Environments: tested, and supported

The package runs the tests and R CMD check on seven CI environments: Ubuntu
with R devel, release, oldrel-1 and 4.2, macOS with release R, Windows
with release R, and Ubuntu with R 4.2 and the suggested packages at their
minimum versions. Before a release, the maintainers also run the tests on
their PC with two R versions. The lowest R is the one `DESCRIPTION` names,
so a newer R feature fails there. R devel shows a change in R that will
break the package.

The suggested packages are tested at two points: at the minimum version
`DESCRIPTION` names for each, in that one CI job, and at the latest
versions, in the other jobs and on the maintainers' PC. Each minimum is the
first version with what the package uses, and
`inst/validation/dependency-minimums.md` says why.

The Quality Plan names what is not tested, and accepts the risk:

- a system without the suggested packages (most jobs install them);
- versions of the suggested packages between the minimum and the latest;
- other operating system versions, other architectures and other locales;
- another RTF reader. The tests compare RTF text. A person opens the
  reference files in Word, and no other reader is checked.

### What the package's evidence covers, and what you do

The package's evidence shows that each function does what its requirements
say, in the environments above. It does not show that the package is fit for
your reports, in your environment, with your standards. That is your
validation. You state your requirements, link each to the FRs it relies on,
run acceptance tests on dummy data in your environment, and sign off. You
use the package's records as supplier evidence. You do not repeat them. The
steps are in [Validating rtfreporter in your
environment](validation.html).

## The document system

### The map

The package's documents form a chain. Each one points to the next by ids.

```
Quality Plan                      the rules; written by hand
   |
Functional Requirements           requirements.csv        FR-PL101, ...
   |
Traceability Matrix  (FR -> FT)   traceability_matrix.csv
   |                              + traceability_review.csv   (the check of each mapping)
Tests and their log               testthat blocks, FT-PL001, ...
   |
Reference outputs                 fixtures/validation/*.rtf
   |                              + reference_review.csv      (the reading of each file)
Deviations                        deviations.csv          (an FR with no test)
   |
Quality Report  (each release)    quality-report-<tag>.pdf + attachments
```

Between major releases, the Change Request Plan and the Change Report take
the place of the Plan and the Report.

### The package's documents, one line each

| Document | What it is |
|---|---|
| Quality Plan | How quality is assured, and what the Quality Report must show. |
| Functional Requirements | `requirements.csv`: every FR, with its kind and the functions it applies to. |
| Traceability Matrix (FR -> FT) | `traceability_matrix.csv`: the tests mapped to each FR. It holds no results. |
| Mapping reviews | `traceability_review.csv`: for each mapping, whether the test asserts the FR, with the evidence. |
| Tests and their log | The testthat tests, and the log of a run. The results are in the log. |
| Reference outputs | The RTF files that the end-to-end tests compare against. |
| Reference reviews | `reference_review.csv`: for each reference RTF, its md5, the verdict, what was checked. |
| Deviations | `deviations.csv`: an FR the tests cannot check, with its risk, the reason it is accepted and the action planned. |
| Quality Report | The conclusion for a release, from 0.9.0 on: the results (overall, by area, the skipped tests with their reasons), the environments run, the supported environments and the tested ones that stand for them, the deviations, how to read the attachments. |
| Change Request Plan | The release's GitHub milestone: each issue with its impact, risk and related FRs. |
| Change Report | The merged pull requests and issues, the FRs added or changed, the regression evidence and the environments. |

The Quality Report concludes *validation-ready* when four things hold. Every
FR with tests passes them. Every FR without a test is a deviation with its
risk and reason. The tests pass on every environment. The changes were made
under the roles of the Quality Plan. Only the CI run of a published release
can conclude *validation-ready*. A run on a PC, or a CI run started by hand,
writes the same report marked DRAFT, and a DRAFT concludes nothing: read the
report attached to the release.

### The company's documents

You make these from the validation kit, `rtfreporter_validation_kit()`.

| Document | What it is |
|---|---|
| Validation Plan | `validation_plan.md`: scope, intended use, roles, approach, acceptance criteria. |
| User Requirement Specification (URS) | `urs.csv`: your requirements (`UR-NNN`), each linked to FR ids. |
| UAT cases | `uat_cases.csv`, `uat_cases.xlsx`: your acceptance tests (`UAT-NNN`) on dummy data, with columns for the result. |
| User Traceability Matrix (URS -> FR -> UAT) | Written by `build_user_matrix.R`. |
| Validation Summary Report | `validation_summary_report.md`: the environment, the results, the deviations, your conclusion. |

The FR ids join the two sides.

```
your need     the package's requirement        the package's test
UR-008  ----> FR-PL161  ----------------------> FT
  |
  +-------->  UAT-011  (your check, in your environment)
```

## Where each document lives, and when it is made

| Document | Where | When |
|---|---|---|
| Quality Plan | `inst/validation/quality-plan.md` in the package; also in the kit | By hand: for the first release under it, and for each major version. |
| Functional Requirements | `inst/validation/requirements.csv`; also in the kit | By hand, with each change that adds or changes an FR. |
| Traceability Matrix | `inst/validation/traceability_matrix.csv`; at a release, `traceability_matrix-<tag>.xlsx` | The CSV is kept with each change. CI writes the workbook at the release. |
| Mapping reviews | `inst/validation/traceability_review.csv` | By hand, when a test is mapped. |
| Reference reviews | `inst/validation/reference_review.csv` | By hand, when a reference is new or written again. |
| Deviations | `inst/validation/deviations.csv` | By hand. A row is removed when a test is added. |
| Tests | `tests/testthat/` in the repository | With each change. |
| Local environment records | `validation/env-local/` in the repository | The maintainers run them before a release. |
| Quality Report | `quality-report-<tag>.pdf`, attached to the GitHub release | CI makes it at a published release, from 0.9.0 on. A CI run started by hand keeps a DRAFT as its artifact `quality-report`. |
| Attachments | The same release: `traceability_matrix-<tag>.xlsx`, `environments-<tag>.txt` (every environment's sessionInfo and test log), `test-log-<tag>.txt`, `ft-<tag>.csv`, `functions-<tag>.csv`, `candidates-<tag>.csv` | CI makes them with the report. |
| Change Request Plan | The release's GitHub milestone | Between major releases. |
| Change Report | The release, between major releases | Made from the merged pull requests and issues; the reasons for deviations by hand. |
| Company documents | The folder you copy with `rtfreporter_validation_kit()` | You make them for each version you validate. |

The package folder `inst/validation/` is installed with the package. The
`validation/` folder of the repository holds the scripts that make the
report, and the local records.

The attachments help you read the report. `traceability_matrix-<tag>.xlsx`
answers which tests check a requirement, `test-log-<tag>.txt` whether they
passed, and `environments-<tag>.txt` what each environment ran with.
`ft-<tag>.csv` has one row per test. `functions-<tag>.csv` has one row
per exported function: its FRs by kind, how many have a test, and the
arguments that no FR names. `candidates-<tag>.csv` lists tests that call a
function but map to no FR. They decide nothing, and they never count as
coverage.

To validate the package for your own use, follow [Validating rtfreporter in
